challenges.title: Ladder 6 · The Orthodox Terms
challenges.summary: Ladder session 6 of 6. The wider Orthodox vocabulary the Christology stands in: Panagia, ousia and energies, the essence-energies distinction, theosis, perichoresis, and prosopon.
challenges.source: 2 Peter 1:4 · John 17:21-23 · St. Gregory Palamas, the Triads

lessons.heading: Panagia, and the map of essence and energies
lessons.body: Panagia (pah-nah-GEE-ah) means All-Holy, the Church's beloved title for Mary — the one whose holiness is wholly gift, as ours is meant to be. Around her, the Damascene and St. Gregory Palamas draw the map this whole ladder stands in. Ousia (oo-SEE-ah), essence, answers what God is: the divine being itself, utterly beyond creaturely comprehension — no one has known, or can know, what God is in himself (Exodus 33:20; 1 Timothy 6:16). The energies (EN-er-jeez) answer what God does: his uncreated operations and gifts — life, light, grace, the glory of Tabor — truly God, truly given. The essence-energies distinction holds both: God is unknowable in essence and genuinely knowable in his energies, as the sun is untouchable in its core and warm on your skin.

lessons.heading: Theosis and perichoresis: where the map leads
lessons.body: Theosis (theh-OH-sis) is the destination: becoming by grace what God is by nature — "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4). Not absorption (the Eutychian ditch in mystical dress) and not moral improvement alone: real participation in the uncreated life, while we remain creatures forever. Perichoresis (peh-ree-koh-REE-sis) names the shape of that life in God himself: the mutual indwelling of the Persons — the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, the Spirit in both — distinct without distance, one without confusion. The same word serves Christology (the natures interpenetrate in the one Person without mixing) and the Trinity, and it is why salvation is pictured as being drawn into a communion that already exists, not admitted to a crowd: "that they all may be one, as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee" (John 17:21).

lessons.heading: Prosopon: the face of the Person
lessons.body: Prosopon (PROH-soh-pon) is the Greek word for face, and in theology for the person as presented — the one you meet, address, and love. It carries both riches and a warning from the ladder's first rungs: in sloppy hands prosopon shrank toward mask or role (the old Sabellian danger, as if the Persons were faces God wears). The councils therefore anchored it: prosopon is true speech when it means hypostasis — a real, distinct who, not a costume. Say the whole ladder back now: one God, one ousia, three hypostases (never three prosopa as masks); in Christ, one hypostasis and prosopon of the Word, two natures with all their idioms, two wills, and the energies of God given to us for theosis. That is the faith of the sessions — hold it, and you can hear any new claim and know within a sentence which ditch it leans toward.

questions.prompt: Panagia means...
choices: Mother of the Trinity
All-Holy — the beloved title of Mary, whose holiness is wholly gift
Queen above the angels by nature
A name for the Church building
questions.explanation: Panagia, All-Holy: the first fruit of the grace the rest of this session describes.

questions.prompt: The essence-energies distinction confesses...
choices: God is partly knowable in his essence if we try hard
God is unknowable in his essence, and truly knowable in his uncreated energies — both, without division
The energies are created effects, so we never meet God himself
Essence and energies are two gods
questions.explanation: Untouchable core, real warmth: we participate in God himself by his energies, while his essence remains forever beyond creatures.

questions.prompt: What is theosis?
choices: Becoming God by essence
Participation in the divine life by grace — becoming by grace what God is by nature, while remaining creatures
Escaping the body and the world as evil
A reward only for monks
questions.explanation: 2 Peter 1:4: partakers of the divine nature. Union without confusion — Chalcedon's pattern applied to our salvation.

questions.prompt: Perichoresis names...
choices: A council procedure
The mutual indwelling of the divine Persons — and, in Christ, of the natures in the one Person — without confusion
The procession of the Spirit only
A style of Byzantine chant
questions.explanation: Distinct without distance, one without confusion. Salvation is being drawn into that existing communion (John 17:21).

questions.prompt: Why did the councils treat prosopon carefully?
choices: It is a Latin word they distrusted
It can shrink toward mask or role; it is safe only when it means hypostasis, a real distinct who
It refers to the human nature only
It was invented by Nestorius
questions.explanation: Face and person — true when anchored to hypostasis, dangerous when it slides toward three masks of one actor.

questions.prompt: Which sentence recites the whole ladder cleanly?
choices: One God in three masks; Christ a God-filled man; salvation by example
One ousia, three hypostases; in Christ one hypostasis of the Word in two natures, two wills, all idioms predicated of the Person; God known in his energies, and we deified by grace
Two persons, one nature, one will; Mary bore a man; God is unknowable entirely
One nature after the union; the essence is given to us as we cease to be creatures
questions.explanation: That is the six sessions in one breath — Godhead, union, properties, heresies avoided, councils, figures, and terms all held together.

challenges.title: Dogma and spirituality
challenges.level: 1 teaching card · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Dogma is not an optional preface to Christian life. Faith and a moral life belong together, and so do doctrine and prayer.

lessons.heading: Dogma and spirituality
lessons.body: A common modern habit treats dogma as optional history and keeps morality or social programs as the real Christian work. That split contradicts the faith itself. James says faith without works is dead. Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law — meaning the old rites and sacrifices, not mercy and obedience. Good deeds do not purchase salvation, and faith does not float free of a moral life. The same is true of doctrine and prayer. Dogma and mysticism lead to the one Truth, who is Christ. Orthodox theology, from Paul and Ignatius to Theophan and Silouan, starts in spiritual experience rather than in a system that never prays. Christianity does not answer every curiosity. It opens a reality before which the soul grows quiet.

challenges.title: Faith, the call, and conversion
challenges.level: 3 teaching cards · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Faith is an encounter God begins. The call can be heard in a noisy life, and conversion has as many paths as there are persons.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: What is faith?
lessons.body: Faith is the path on which we meet God, and God takes the first step. He believes in us before we believe in Him, and gives some sign of His presence. Our first move is an answer. The Galilean fishermen drop their nets at “Follow me.” The rich young man hears the same call and goes away sad, because he has treasure on earth. Poverty of spirit is the blessing: to know that nothing you own can stand in for God, and to hunger for Him with soul, mind, and will.

lessons.heading: The call
lessons.body: The call is easy to miss. A life filled with work can leave no silence in which God is heard, and religion can shrink to a holiday kept for the sake of roots. Even so, the call still comes — sometimes only as restlessness. Augustine’s line belongs here: we were made for God, and our hearts are restless until they rest in Him. The costly mistake is to recognize the voice years after it spoke. Answer when He speaks. That answer can transfigure a whole life.

lessons.heading: Conversion to God
lessons.body: No two people come to God by the same road. The meeting may be sudden or slow, in childhood or in old age. Often the seeker thinks he has found God, and later sees that God found him. Augustine’s long reading, a collapse of health or hope, the face of a believer, or a religious family — all of these are real paths, and none of them is automatic. Faith received from one’s parents still has to become one’s own. Faith is a gift. It is often given through the effort of the person who asked for it.

questions.prompt: Who takes the first step in faith?
choices: God, who gives a sign of His presence
The believer, who must become worthy first
No one; faith is a guess
questions.explanation: Faith is an encounter God opens. Our first step is a response.

questions.prompt: How may God’s call arrive in a noisy life?

questions.explanation: The call can feel like dissatisfaction or a search, and only later be recognized as God. Augustine: the heart is restless until it rests in Him.

choices: There is one approved path, and every believer must copy it
Every path is personal, and even a family faith must become one’s own

questions.explanation: No two roads are the same. Faith is a gift, often given through the seeker’s own effort, and inherited faith still has to be personally lived.

challenges.title: From philosophy to revelation
challenges.level: 2 teaching cards · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Greek thought came near the truth and then stopped. Israel knew God because God spoke and walked with a people.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: Philosophy in search of a supreme Good
lessons.body: From the beginning, people have hunted for the meaning of being. Greek philosophy studied the world, the mind, and the first causes, and often joined that study to ascetic discipline, a purification of mind and body. The order of things — the cosmos, as against chaos — suggested a Maker. Plato could speak of Creator, Father, and Craftsman, and of the Logos. Plotinus pressed further: the One beyond every definition, then Intelligence and Soul, a triad, with the world as a reflection of the divine. Early Christian writers could call such philosophers Christians before Christ. Near is not the same as arrival. Philosophy can see the foothills. It cannot climb the mountain by itself.

lessons.heading: The Old Testament: divine revelation
lessons.body: Most of the ancient world worshipped many gods. Israel was entrusted with something else: knowledge of God, of creation, and of why we exist, learned not only from books but from a long experience. Noah, Abraham, Moses, Elijah, and the righteous of Israel spoke with God and walked before Him. This God is not an abstract force. He speaks, hears, and acts. He goes before the people as fire, and He consents to dwell in the house they build, though heaven and earth cannot contain Him. The God of the philosophers stays distant and lifeless by comparison. Both paths confess that God is a mystery. Philosophy stops at the foothills. Revelation takes people up the mountain.

questions.prompt: Why did some early Christians call Greek philosophers “Christians before Christ”?
choices: Because Plato and Plotinus had already come near the one God, the Logos, and a divine triad
Because Greek religion was already the Church
Because philosophy replaces the Bible
questions.explanation: They came near: one Maker, the Logos, a triad, the vision of God. Near is not yet revelation.

questions.prompt: How did Israel know God, in this reading?
choices: By age-long encounter: God spoke, led, and dwelt among them
Only by copying Greek metaphysics
By concluding that God is an impersonal law
questions.explanation: Revelation is personal. The God of Israel is living and near, and still mysterious.

questions.prompt: Where does philosophy stop, and revelation go on?
choices: Philosophy remains at the foothills; revelation leads up the mountain
They teach exactly the same thing
Revelation forbids anyone to think
questions.explanation: Both confess the mystery. Only revelation brings a person into the presence of the living God.

lessons.heading: The angels

Gregory of Nyssa reads the parable of the lost sheep with the same map: the ninety-nine who never left the hills are the angels, and the one sheep the shepherd seeks is the human race. Human beings are not angels, and angels are not a substitute for the Incarnation. God assumed human nature, not an angelic one. Honor the angels as fellow servants who praise God and care for the race He came to save.

challenges.title: The origin of evil
challenges.level: 2 teaching cards · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Evil is not a second god and not a substance. It begins in a created will that turns away, and it becomes active in the devil and the demons.

challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: The origin of evil
lessons.body: Before the visible world, and after the angels were made, a catastrophe struck, known now by its wreckage. Angels were meant to grow in virtue until they were as like God as a creature can be. Some refused. From then on the world is a field of two unequal powers: God, and the devil who is not His rival equal. Dualism is the mistake to refuse — the idea that light and darkness, spirit and matter, are two eternal kingdoms. Matter is not evil. Evil is not a substance that has always existed. Basil says it plainly: evil is not a living substance but a condition of the soul, as shadow is the absence of light. Lucifer was created good. He ruined his own goodness by the freedom he was given, and fell from the Source of good.

lessons.heading: The evil-doer
lessons.body: Evil has no being of its own. It becomes an agent of ruin when it is taken up into a person: the devil and the demons. That is what it means to say evil was “hypostasized.” It is still a parasite on good. Scripture can speak of God “creating evil” or sending a lying spirit, and those lines have to be read without making God the author of wickedness. He remains Lord over good and evil in the sense that He can allow an evil will and bend its consequences toward good. His thoughts are not our thoughts. The devil is real, defeated in advance, and not a second creator.

A god equal to the God of light, ruling matter forever
The material world itself
questions.explanation: Evil is a falling away from good, not a coeternal substance. Matter is not the evil kingdom.

questions.prompt: How did the devil become the devil?

questions.explanation: Lucifer was created good. The fall of the angels is a misuse of freedom, not God’s design.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that evil was “hypostasized”?
choices: It became active in persons — the devil and the demons — without ever becoming a real substance of its own
It became a second god
It ceased to exist
questions.explanation: Evil has no independent being. It becomes an agent only in a created will that has turned.

challenges.title: The human person
challenges.level: 3 teaching cards · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Humanity is the crown of creation: one nature of soul and body, free, made in the image of God, and called onward to likeness.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: The human person
lessons.body: Human beings are the crown of the making of the world. Before Adam, the Persons take counsel: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.” The body is formed from the ground, and then God breathes the breath of life. We are not angels housed in a costume, and we are not animals with no spirit. The honor is shown by what the Son later assumed: not an angelic nature, but ours. Every human person stands at the center of the creation God loves.

lessons.heading: Image and likeness
lessons.body: God did not make a solitary self. He made male and female, because a closed monad cannot love, and love is what the image is for. The image includes freedom. God will not force a person into good or into evil; that force would cancel the image. Likeness is the calling still ahead: Gregory of Nyssa says the limit of a life of virtue is becoming like God. You are already the image. You are not yet finished. The Christian life is the road from image to likeness, and it is walked in freedom.

lessons.heading: Soul and body
lessons.body: Christian faith agrees that the person is soul and body, and refuses the dualist conclusion that matter is evil and the body a prison. When Paul speaks of flesh warring against spirit, he is naming disordered desire, not condemning the body God made and will raise. Asceticism trains the body; it does not hate it. The end is higher than escape. The human person is called to become god by grace — not by nature, and not by leaving the body behind, but by union with God in the whole person He created.

questions.prompt: What does “Let us make” reveal about the human person?
choices: The Trinity’s counsel, and a creature made in God’s image
A bargain among the angels
That humanity is an accident of matter
questions.explanation: The Persons take counsel together. Humanity is the crown of creation, breathed into life by God.

questions.prompt: How do image and likeness differ here?
choices: The image is given, including freedom; likeness is the virtue we are called to grow into
They are opposites, and the image is lost forever
Likeness means God forces the will
questions.explanation: Freedom belongs to the image. Gregory of Nyssa: the limit of virtue is assimilation to God. God does not force the choice.

questions.prompt: What does this reading refuse about the body?
choices: That matter is originally evil and the body a prison
That soul and body are both real
That desire can be disordered
questions.explanation: Christianity rejects the dualist hatred of matter. The body is for salvation. Flesh against spirit names disordered desire, not a cursed creation.

challenges.title: Before the Fall, and the Fall
challenges.level: 2 teaching cards · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: The first humans were blessed and able to praise God. The Fall is their misuse of freedom, by pride, not a defect God built into them.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: Primordial humanity before the Fall
lessons.body: A materialist picture says the first humans were simply clever animals, without God and without morality. The Church confesses the opposite: a first blessedness, a life with God in Paradise, a nature able to praise Him in words — something no other creature does. That original integrity is not a fairy tale tacked onto history. It is the memory of what we were made to be. Evil was not woven into the design. The possibility of turning away was the shadow side of a real freedom.

lessons.heading: The Fall
lessons.body: The story of the Fall is the pattern of our whole history: who we were, and what we became. Evil entered the world not because God willed it but because human beings preferred the devil’s lie to God’s command. Freedom made them the image of the Maker, and freedom held the possibility of falling. God would not override that freedom, and the devil could not force the sin. The fault is ours. Augustine names the sin as disobedience. Most of the early Fathers name it as pride: the self turning in on itself. The tree is suddenly “good for food” and “a delight to the eyes,” and God is pushed out of the center. Every generation repeats the swap — my desire first, God forgotten.

questions.prompt: What does the Church confess about the first humans?
choices: A blessed life with God, able to praise Him, not a merely bestial beginning
That God created them already fallen
That they were angels who later became animals
questions.explanation: Against the materialist picture, the faith confesses original blessedness and a real capacity to praise God.

questions.prompt: Who bears responsibility for the Fall?
choices: Human beings, who misused a freedom God would not override
God, who willed the evil
The devil, who forced them
questions.explanation: God did not will the evil and would not cancel freedom. The devil could not compel it. The misuse is human.

questions.prompt: What do most early Fathers name as Adam’s sin?
choices: Pride, the self turned inward
A lack of intelligence
The creation of the body
questions.explanation: Augustine stresses disobedience. The wider early tradition stresses pride: God is no longer the center; one’s own desire is.

lessons.heading: The attributes of the Church
lessons.body: “I believe in one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Church” is not a slogan. It names a divine-human organism. She is one because she is built in the image of the Trinity: unity of essence, and real persons who are not dissolved. She is holy because the Holy One dwells in her, even while her members are still being healed. She is catholic because she holds the whole faith for the whole world, not because she is merely large. She is apostolic because she continues the apostles’ teaching and mission. Christians are in patria and in via at once — already home, and still on the way. Lands that were once Christian can become mission fields again. The four marks are a confession, not a boast that the members have finished becoming holy.

Because disagreement is impossible

lessons.heading: The church hierarchy

The faithful are told to honor it: deacons as servants of Christ’s commandments, bishops as those who stand in the Church in a way that Ignatius can even say “as Jesus Christ” in the sense of representing His authority, not of replacing Him. Honor is not a free pass. Paul tells Timothy, newly ordained, to be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity. The hierarchy exists for the altar and the flock. A leader who will not serve has forgotten the order he was given.

lessons.heading: Women in the Church

That is not a doctrine of women’s uselessness. Women bake the Eucharistic bread, read, sing, and carry works as necessary as those of the early deaconesses. The Mother of God is the Church’s measure of how highly a woman is honored. The argument is about the shape of the priestly office, not about the worth of women.

lessons.heading: Church time
lessons.body: The Church is on earth and turned toward heaven; she lives in time and breathes eternity. That double life is why there is a calendar. The year, the week, and the day are not empty schedules. They are how communion with eternity is practiced. In the feasts, the events of Christ’s life become the experience of the person who is praying, not only a memory of someone else’s past. As an icon carries the presence of the one depicted, church time carries the presence of Christ, His Mother, the angels, and the saints whose memory is kept. Skip the calendar and you do not become more spiritual. You become deaf to the way the Church has learned to stand in both time and eternity.

challenges.title: The Church and the churches

lessons.heading: Divisions and reconciliation
lessons.body: The Creed says one Church. The world is full of communities that use the name and often refuse one another Communion. The early Church was severe with heresy: no shared Eucharist, no shared prayer, because Arius, Sabellius, and Eutyches denied the foundations — Christ’s divinity, the equality of the Persons, the fullness of the two natures. Most communities Christians meet today are not in that category. They accept the basic dogmas. Philaret of Moscow said that treating Catholicism as if it were Arianism is harsh and useless. Separated communities can be regarded as branches cut from the trunk, and at the same time an Orthodox Christian must not announce that God is forbidden to act outside the Orthodox Church. That would cage the Almighty. Augustine’s caution belongs with Philaret’s: on the day of judgment, some who seemed outside will be found within, and some who seemed within will not. God knows the limits of the Church. We do not get to finish His sentence.

They used a different calendar only

challenges.title: A life in the sacraments
challenges.level: 1 teaching card · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: A sacrament is an encounter: a visible rite and a material gift, and an invisible rebirth of the whole person, body and soul.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: A life in the sacraments
lessons.body: The sacraments are sacred actions in which God and a person meet. Grace descends and sanctifies. The Orthodox Church speaks of seven — Baptism, Chrismation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing, Marriage, and Priesthood — and treats other sacred actions as rites. That numbering was learned from Latin scholasticism. The Fathers of the first millennium did not anxiously count. What they did know is the shape of each mystery: a visible side (words, gestures, and a material — water, bread, wine, oil) and an invisible side, the person’s transfiguration, which is the mystery proper. The body is not left outside. Immersion, anointing, and communion are bodily because the body is meant for salvation and deification. In the age to come the material signs will no longer be needed in the same way. Here, they are how God gives Himself to people who are still body and soul.

The prayer of faith will save the sick; the Lord will raise him up; if he has sinned, he will be forgiven. Healing and forgiveness are one visit. lessons.heading: Priesthood
lessons.body: The sacrament of priesthood is conferred in three rites: to the episcopate, to the priesthood, and to the diaconate. In present Orthodox practice bishops are chosen from the monks. The early Church also had married bishops; the later discipline is a received rule of life, not a denial that marriage is holy. At the ordination the Church sings “Lord, have mercy” while the bishop reads the prayers. The point of those prayers is that the gift comes from God. A contrast makes it sharp: in some Protestant settings the only difference between lay and ordained is a license to preach. Orthodox ordination is not that. It sets a man at the altar to offer the Eucharist and to shepherd, by a gift he cannot give himself.

lessons.heading: Monasticism
lessons.body: The Orthodox rite of monastic tonsure has a sacramental character. Dionysius and the rite itself call it a mystery. Like baptism, it is a death to a merely fleshly life and a new beginning. Its aim is the chastity and wholeness Adam and Eve had before the Fall — “a life according to the Gospel,” the Fathers said, and “a true philosophy.” The Lord’s own words are its rule: sell what you have, deny yourself, take up the cross, love Him more than father and mother. A monk is the merchant who sells everything for the one pearl. Monasticism was in the Church early and came to the fore in the fourth century, when martyrdom was no longer the ordinary threat and the empire made peace with the faith. The desert became a way to die to the world without waiting for a persecutor. It is one path, as marriage and priesthood are paths. Walked to the end, it leads to salvation and deification. It is not a higher caste of Christians, and it is not an escape from love.

choices: As a mystery, a death to fleshly life like baptism
As a hobby with no rite

questions.explanation: The rite and Dionysius call tonsure a sacrament. It is a death and a beginning, akin to baptism.

lessons.heading: The Last Judgment
lessons.body: At death the soul leaves the body and does not lose memory, thought, or feeling. It enters the other world carrying the weight of its life. lessons.heading: What is hell?

Sophrony says he does not see Christ as Michelangelo painted Him, hurling people into the abyss. He sees Christ immensely powerful with the power of unassuming love — and if God is love, He is love even while He judges. Hell is bound to Holy Week and Pascha: Christ descends into the abyss, as He descended into the Jordan, and hell cannot bear His light. It surrenders its prisoners. Hell is real. It is also already sentenced to death. Fear is a poor teacher beside that invasion of love.
